---
title: "Feelings towards the parties"
description: "How young people in the UK rate five parties, and how this differs by age, gender and survey."
date: 2026-11-24
categories: [Parties, Age, Gender]
image: thumbnail.png
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "site.R"))

share <- \(x) percent(mean(x), accuracy = 1)

party_names <- c(
  ftp1_UK = "Conservatives",
  ftp2_UK = "Labour",
  ftp3_UK = "Liberal Democrats",
  ftp4_UK = "Greens",
  ftp5_UK = "Reform UK"
)

# one row per respondent and party
ratings <- respondents |>
  select(dataset, age, age_group, gender, starts_with("ftp")) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("ftp"), names_to = "party", values_to = "rating") |>
  mutate(party = factor(party_names[party], levels = party_names))

# shares that like (7 to 10) or dislike (0 to 3) a party, by survey
like_dislike <- ratings |>
  summarise(
    like = mean(rating >= 7),
    dislike = mean(rating <= 3),
    zero = mean(rating == 0),
    mean = mean(rating),
    .by = c(dataset, party)
  )

stat <- \(data, ds, p, column, f = percent) {
  f(data[[column]][data$dataset == ds & data$party == p], accuracy = 1)
}

# average of all five ratings, in Survation W1 and the range of the others
overall_mean <- ratings |>
  summarise(mean = mean(rating), .by = dataset)
mean_sw1 <- number(overall_mean$mean[overall_mean$dataset == "Survation W1"], accuracy = 0.1)
mean_others <- number(range(overall_mean$mean[overall_mean$dataset != "Survation W1"]), accuracy = 0.1)

# Gallup W2 by age group
gallup_w2_age <- ratings |>
  filter(dataset == "Gallup W2") |>
  summarise(mean = mean(rating), like = mean(rating >= 7), .by = c(age_group, party))

w2_age <- \(ag, p, column, f = number, accuracy = 0.1) {
  f(gallup_w2_age[[column]][gallup_w2_age$age_group == ag & gallup_w2_age$party == p], accuracy = accuracy)
}

# gender differences (men minus women) in the average rating
gender_gap <- ratings |>
  filter(gender %in% c("Female", "Male")) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(rating), .by = c(dataset, party, gender)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = gender, values_from = mean) |>
  mutate(gap = Male - Female)

gap_range <- \(p) {
  gender_gap |>
    filter(party == p) |>
    pull(gap) |>
    range() |>
    number(accuracy = 0.1)
}
green_gap <- gender_gap |>
  filter(party == "Greens") |>
  select(dataset, gap) |>
  deframe() |>
  abs() |>
  number(accuracy = 0.1)

# Gallup respondents aged 18 to 21 in both waves
gallup_1821 <- ratings |>
  filter(dataset %in% c("Gallup W1", "Gallup W2"), age %in% 18:21) |>
  summarise(
    like = mean(rating >= 7),
    dislike = mean(rating <= 3),
    zero = mean(rating == 0),
    .by = c(dataset, party)
  )
n_1821 <- respondents |>
  filter(dataset %in% c("Gallup W1", "Gallup W2"), age %in% 18:21) |>
  count(dataset) |>
  deframe() |>
  comma()
```

```{r}
#| label: thumbnail
#| include: false
# Card image for the listings: the like and dislike bars of the first figure,
# pooled over the surveys, without text
thumbnail <- ratings |>
  summarise(like = mean(rating >= 7), dislike = -mean(rating <= 3), .by = party) |>
  pivot_longer(c(like, dislike)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = fct_rev(party), fill = name)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = brand[["ink"]], linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(like = brand[["blue-dark"]], dislike = brand[["coral-dark"]]), guide = "none") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = brand[["tint"]], colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(24, 40, 24, 40)
  )

ggsave("thumbnail.png", thumbnail, width = 6, height = 3.9, dpi = 150)
```

Most respondents are too young to vote, so their feelings towards the parties are one of the few ways to see how they relate to party politics. All four surveys asked them to rate five parties from 0 (strongly dislike) to 10 (strongly like). Gallup W1 was fielded during the 2024 general election campaign, under a Conservative government, while all later surveys took place after Labour had come to power (see [Who took part](/insights/uk/who-took-part/index.qmd)).

## Which parties young people like

::: {.how-to-read}
Each panel shows one survey. Bars to the right give the share of respondents who rate a party 7 or higher, bars to the left the share who rate it 3 or lower. Ratings of 4 to 6 are not shown.
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-like
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-alt: "Diverging bar charts of the share of respondents who like (7 to 10) and dislike (0 to 3) each of five parties, one panel per survey. Labour is liked by the largest share in Gallup W1 and both Survation surveys, the Greens in Gallup W2. The Conservatives and Reform UK are disliked by the largest shares in Gallup W1, Gallup W2 and Survation W2. In Survation W1 all parties are liked by more and disliked by fewer respondents than in the other surveys."
like_long <- like_dislike |>
  select(dataset, party, like, dislike) |>
  pivot_longer(c(like, dislike), names_to = "side", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(
    value = if_else(side == "dislike", -share, share),
    side = factor(side, levels = c("dislike", "like"), labels = c("Dislike (0 to 3)", "Like (7 to 10)"))
  )

ggplot(like_long, aes(x = value, y = fct_rev(party), fill = side)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = brand[["ink"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = percent(share, accuracy = 1),
      hjust = if_else(value < 0, 1.15, -0.15)
    ),
    size = 3.3,
    colour = brand[["ink"]]
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~dataset, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(brand[["coral-dark"]], brand[["blue-dark"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(-0.72, 0.72),
    breaks = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5),
    labels = \(x) percent(abs(x))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Labour is the party liked most often in three of the four surveys",
    x = "Share of respondents",
    y = NULL,
    caption = site_caption
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    legend.location = "plot",
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1, "cm")
  )
```

Labour is liked by the largest share of respondents in Gallup W1 (`r stat(like_dislike, "Gallup W1", "Labour", "like")`) and in both Survation surveys. Gallup W2 is the exception, where `r stat(like_dislike, "Gallup W2", "Greens", "like")` like the Greens and `r stat(like_dislike, "Gallup W2", "Labour", "like")` like Labour. The Conservatives and Reform UK are disliked most often. In Gallup W1, `r stat(like_dislike, "Gallup W1", "Conservatives", "dislike")` rate the Conservatives 3 or lower, and in both second waves Reform UK receives a rating of 0 more often than any other party (`r stat(like_dislike, "Gallup W2", "Reform UK", "zero")` in Gallup W2, `r stat(like_dislike, "Survation W2", "Reform UK", "zero")` in Survation W2). Yet `r stat(like_dislike, "Survation W2", "Reform UK", "like")` of Survation W2 respondents like Reform UK, about as many as like the Greens, which suggests that Reform UK divides young people more sharply than other parties.

Survation W1 stands apart. Its respondents like every party more often and dislike every party less often, with an average rating of `r mean_sw1` across all five parties, against `r mean_others[1]` to `r mean_others[2]` in the other surveys. This fits their tendency to give higher answers on 0 to 10 scales, so the order of the parties within this survey is a safer guide than their levels.

## Age

::: {.how-to-read}
Each panel shows one party. The dots give the average rating in each age group of a survey. Groups with fewer than 50 respondents are left out.
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-age
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-alt: "Average party ratings by age group and survey, one panel per party. Within Gallup W2, respondents aged 22 to 26 rate the Conservatives, Labour and Reform UK about one point higher than those aged 18 to 21, while ratings of the Greens differ little by age. Within the Survation surveys, 16 and 17 year olds rate all parties slightly lower than 12 to 15 year olds."
age_means <- ratings |>
  summarise(mean = mean(rating), n = n(), .by = c(dataset, age_group, party)) |>
  filter(n >= 50)

ggplot(age_means, aes(x = age_group, y = mean, colour = dataset, group = dataset)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5, colour = brand[["rule"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  facet_wrap(~party, ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dataset_colours, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2.5, 6.5), breaks = 3:6) +
  labs(
    title = "In Gallup W2, 22 to 26 year olds rate most parties higher",
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Average rating (0 to 10)",
    caption = site_caption
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.84, 0.22),
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10)
  )
```

Because the surveys cover different age ranges, age differences are best read within a survey. In Gallup W2, 22 to 26 year olds rate the Conservatives at `r w2_age("22-26", "Conservatives", "mean")` on average, against `r w2_age("18-21", "Conservatives", "mean")` among 18 to 21 year olds, and Reform UK at `r w2_age("22-26", "Reform UK", "mean")` against `r w2_age("18-21", "Reform UK", "mean")`. They also rate Labour higher, while ratings of the Greens hardly differ by age. As the older group rates almost every party more warmly, this could partly reflect a general tendency to rate higher rather than a preference for particular parties. In the Survation surveys the pattern runs the other way, as 16 and 17 year olds rate all five parties slightly lower than 12 to 15 year olds.

## Gender

::: {.how-to-read}
Each row compares the average rating of a party among young women and young men in one survey. A longer line means a larger gap.
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-gender
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-alt: "Dumbbell charts of the average party ratings of young women and young men, one panel per survey. In all four surveys young men rate the Conservatives and Reform UK higher than young women. In both Gallup surveys young women rate the Greens higher than young men. Gaps for Labour and the Liberal Democrats are smaller and less consistent."
gender_means <- ratings |>
  filter(gender %in% c("Female", "Male")) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(rating), .by = c(dataset, party, gender))

ggplot(gender_means, aes(x = mean, y = fct_rev(party))) +
  geom_line(aes(group = party), colour = brand[["rule"]], linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = gender), size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~dataset, ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = gender_colours, breaks = c("Female", "Male"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(2.5, 6.5), breaks = 3:6) +
  labs(
    title = "Young men rate the Conservatives and Reform UK higher than young women",
    x = "Average rating (0 to 10)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = site_caption
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    legend.location = "plot",
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1, "cm")
  )
```

In all four surveys, young men rate the Conservatives higher than young women, by `r gap_range("Conservatives")[1]` to `r gap_range("Conservatives")[2]` points, and Reform UK by `r gap_range("Reform UK")[1]` to `r gap_range("Reform UK")[2]` points. In turn, young women in the two Gallup surveys rate the Greens higher, by `r green_gap[["Gallup W1"]]` points in W1 and `r green_gap[["Gallup W2"]]` points in W2. The gaps for Labour and the Liberal Democrats are smaller and less consistent, and in Survation W1 young men rate every party somewhat higher.

## The same ages in two waves

::: {.how-to-read}
Both panels compare Gallup respondents aged 18 to 21 in W1 (spring 2024, light blue) and W2 (mostly late 2025, dark blue). A longer line means a larger difference between the two surveys.
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-waves
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-alt: "Dot charts comparing Gallup respondents aged 18 to 21 in W1 and W2. The share who like Labour is lower in W2 and the share who like the Greens is higher. The share who dislike Labour and Reform UK is higher in W2. The other shares change little."
waves <- gallup_1821 |>
  select(dataset, party, like, dislike) |>
  pivot_longer(c(like, dislike), names_to = "side", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(side = factor(side, levels = c("like", "dislike"), labels = c("Like (7 to 10)", "Dislike (0 to 3)")))

waves_wide <- waves |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = dataset, values_from = share)

ggplot(waves, aes(x = share, y = fct_rev(party))) +
  geom_segment(
    data = waves_wide,
    aes(x = `Gallup W1`, xend = `Gallup W2`, yend = fct_rev(party)),
    colour = brand[["rule"]],
    linewidth = 2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = dataset), size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~side, ncol = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = dataset_colours, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(), limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  labs(
    title = "Fewer 18 to 21 year olds liked Labour in W2, and more liked the Greens",
    x = "Share of respondents aged 18 to 21",
    y = NULL,
    caption = site_caption
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    legend.location = "plot",
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(1, "cm")
  )
```

The Gallup surveys allow a fairer comparison over time, as both include over 800 respondents aged 18 to 21 (`r n_1821[["Gallup W1"]]` and `r n_1821[["Gallup W2"]]`) recruited in the same way. In this age group, the share who like Labour falls from `r stat(gallup_1821, "Gallup W1", "Labour", "like")` in W1 to `r stat(gallup_1821, "Gallup W2", "Labour", "like")` in W2, while the share who like the Greens rises from `r stat(gallup_1821, "Gallup W1", "Greens", "like")` to `r stat(gallup_1821, "Gallup W2", "Greens", "like")`. The share who like Reform UK hardly changes, but the share who rate it 0 rises from `r stat(gallup_1821, "Gallup W1", "Reform UK", "zero")` to `r stat(gallup_1821, "Gallup W2", "Reform UK", "zero")`. The two surveys lie on either side of the change of government. However, they consist of different young people, so the data cannot tell whether the differences reflect the events of that period or who happened to take part.

Gallup W1 also introduced the parties with slightly different wording, so small differences between surveys should be read with care. [The data](/data.qmd) page describes how the surveys differ.
